utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone as well. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. That's going to be Mr. Bego Salimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No protective measures, and we will be seeking to have his statements filed as exhibits under Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Has the 89(F) summary been presented to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is there any problem as far as the 89(F) summary is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, will you please escort Mr. Selimovic into the courtroom. Then, Ms. Edgerton, perhaps, since we are waiting for the witness to arrive, I received an explanatory e-mail about the different versions of the -- could you please look at the second last line, whether the number 0986 at the very end is correct or whether that should be 0980.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I have no idea what it is Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, well - we'll come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Selimovic. Mr. Selimovic, you will first be examined by Ms. Edgerton, who represents the Prosecution in this case. But before I give you an opportunity to do so, Ms. Edgerton, do I understand that a copy of this e-mail of the 18th of March has not been given, this explanatory e-mail has not been given to the Defence? There's nothing special in it. It just explains what versions of statements were used and what versions were retrieved. Would it be possible to give a copy to Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I have a copy here that I can hand over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you can do that. And I think there's nothing that -- there's no specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, indeed, I wasn't even sure I didn't have it. I absolutely didn't even know what it was that was being referred to, Your Honour. That was my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might not have been sufficiently clear. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just with regard to the question you asked before, and this may assist Mr. Stewart by way of some explanation, attached to Mr. Selimovic's statement to the ICTY of 1997 was a barely legible copy of a statement he had given to Bosnian authorities in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the point and, in fact, am rather relieved that nobody sent me this e-mail. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That took me a while as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, perhaps you can check on the second last line, the last four digits, whether it should be 0986 or 0980?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It should be 0980, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That might well solve everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I always regret that it's the Chamber that has to find these incorrect references but let's not spend too much time o on it. Mr. Selimovic, this has got nothing to do with you. It was all bureaucracy. And now Ms. Edgerton will examine you as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Edgerton:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic? Good afternoon, Mr. Selimovic.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, you, I understand, have given statements about your experiences in 1992 both to Bosnian authorities and to representatives of the ICTY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, what about establishing, first of all, the identity of the witness. Would that be a good suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, could you give the Court your name, and tell us your date of birth and your place of residence in the years leading up to the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: My name is Bego Selimovic, from Gornja Bioca. I was born on the 21st of January, 1950, and I resided in Gornja Bioca, where I was born. This is in Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selimovic. Now, have you given statements about your experiences in 1992 both to authorities of your country and to representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on two of those statements, one that you gave in 1993 - and the for the Court, that would be the statement with the ERN number 00987804 to 00987808 - and the one given to the ICTY in 1997. Before you appeared in court this afternoon, did you have a chance to read these statements from 1993 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to reading them, and because you have some trouble with your eyes that means you have a hard time reading fine print, were those statements also read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you understand what you read and what was read back to you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask that the witness be shown the copies in his language of those statements, please, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, then, the witness is shown the more legible but non-corrected version of his 1993 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does he have both the copies there, the 1993 and the 1997? Your Honour, with this witness, I'd just like to hear that he recognises these before they're given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, are those your statements?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps now they could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement dated 5 April 1993 will be Prosecution Exhibit P555. The witness statement dated June 21, 1997 will be Prosecution Exhibit P556.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, specifically here I'd like to have the ERN numbers read out as well, because there are different versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For both statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly of the 1993 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement dated 5 April 1993, the English translation bears ERN number ET-0098-7804-0098-7808, and the B/C/S bears ERN number 0098-87804 to 808.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Selimovic, do you find, or did you find those statements to be correct and a true recording of what you saw and lived through in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand from you that you'd like, in court, to make some small modifications and corrections to both those documents. Shall I read those out to you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your statement to the Tribunal, you referred to the killing of your brother Uzeir, and you wanted to make it clear that you were told he had been killed on the 30th of May but you only learned what had happened to him on the 31st of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement to the Tribunal, you wanted to clarify that when you were moved from the school at Gornja Bioca to Podlugovi, there were only two policemen there but there were four soldiers on the bus you were taken in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the statement you gave in 1993, the earlier statement, in paragraph 6 of that earlier statement, you wanted to clarify that Nafa, the woman named Nafa, referred to there is your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I should note that in the English version, there's an error that should be corrected. It reads "daughter-in-law", so a correction should be made to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also, Mr. Selimovic, in this same paragraph, you noticed a typographical error when they referred to the nickname of your brother's son; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd like that nickname to read "Vajta", V-a-j-t-a, instead of "Vjata" as it appears in the original version?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Vajta, yes, Vajta.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I should note for the Chamber that the English translation in that regard is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your earlier statement, when you mentioned the person who came to the camp in Podlugovi with Vasilja Stolica, you wanted to indicate that this person who came with Stolica gave his name as Mico and said his name was Seselj Jevac [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, you wanted to correct paragraph 32 of that earlier statement because the date noted there that you were transferred to Kula is listed as 8 February and you want to say that it was 9 February?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th we went to Kula, on the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those, Mr. Selimovic, are the corrections that we discussed and went through prior to your testifying here this afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to now like to read in a summary of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, would your summary and would the statements tendered include the periods in 1993? That's a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in the limited regard of his having been asked to bury the bodies of some persons who were found on the side of the road and his release from Kula in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the release from -- well, you said his release from Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Transferred to and released from Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, if you're detained within the limits of the indictment period, I can imagine that what follows that release is relevant in relation to that. But if you are sent only outside the indictment period to Kula, what's the relevance, then, of ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be arguing, Your Honour, that the facilities at Kula were part of an interconnected detention system in Sarajevo, operating under the same authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then you -- I do understand that and I think we heard some evidence on Kula before the 1st of January, 1993. But what would anything after 1993 add to that evidence, and to what extent would that be relevant apart from the fact that it did not stop to exist and that people were still sent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That, in fact, would be it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's proceed first. We'll later consider whether this is of relevance for this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just if I may, I did discuss this procedure in detail with Mr. Selimovic, and he indicated it was very important to him that the Trial Chamber receive the whole body of the evidence as contained in his statement. So keeping that in mind, I submitted the statements without any redaction at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that would be a convincing argument is another matter or whether there would be need to explain to Mr. Selimovic - - well, the limits of a criminal case. But let's proceed at this moment and not, in the presence of Mr. Selimovic, discuss the matter any further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness, Bego Selimovic, is a Muslim from Gornja Bioca, in Ilijas municipality, Sarajevo area. The village of Gornja Bioca was a mixed community pre-war with a distinct Muslim and Serb part. Gornja Bioca bordered the village of Ahatovici, which was a Muslim village, on its eastern side, and the village of Malesici, which was a Serb village to the north. On the south was Vlakovo, which was Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness worked as a security guard in a factory in Stari Ilijas before the war. The witness stopped going to work around 28th April, 1992. From the time he stopped working, the witness, together with men of his village, kept guard because of sporadic shooting into Gornja Bioca. The night of 28 May 1992, Gornja Bioca came under infantry fire and then shelling. The shooting went on for a couple of days. By 30 May, the witness ran out of food and water at his guard post. He went to his house to get supplies. He didn't find any members of his family at home. While in the village, shells exploded nearby. He returned to his guard post where they were joined by other guards who told the witness they had been seen the Serb forces enter Gornja Bioca. Serb forces started shooting in the woods where the witness and others were hiding. The next morning, the witness decided to go back to Bioca. There, he saw his brother Uzeir's family and was told by his daughter-in-law Nafa that Serb forces had killed Uzeir and Uzeir's son on the doorstep of their home. Nafa and his brother's son, Zihad, named one Srpko Pustivuk, among others, as responsible for the killing. The witness returned to the woods and found his wife and family hiding in a little stream with eight or ten men and about 30 women and children. They remained there until 1 June, when Serb forces started shooting from both sides. The villagers were surrounded and taken by Serb forces to the primary school in Bioca where they met others who had surrendered. All together, the witness believes there were about 60 detainees in the school. The men detained at the primary school were eventually transferred to a school in Podlugovi by armed men who wore camouflage uniforms. On arriving at the school, the detainees were placed in three rooms. They found people from Ljesevo there, including about five women. There were also people from Crnotina, which was in Ilijas. Between all three rooms at this Podlugovi school, there must have been 100 detainees. There was a toilet but no water, lice, and for Bajram, the detainees received no food for two days. After that, they used to get a quarter loaf of bread per person every 24 hours. The chief of the detention facility was called Slavko. One day, just before dark, Vasilja Stolica from Kralup came together with a Serb that was armed with a gun and a hammer. They asked two people from among the prisoners to go with them. One Bakir Sehic moved a bit. They tied him up and took him away. He was never seen again. Around 16 August 1992, the gaol commander let a man who introduced himself as the minister of justice inside the school together with two policemen. This man told the detainees they were going to be moved to Semizovac. He told them they would have good food and accommodation and they would be taken for work. While the man who introduced him as minister of justice was in civilian clothes, the witness saw that the two policemen wore camouflage uniforms and had marks on their sleeves saying "Serb Police". The detainees from the school were loaded onto a bus by policemen in uniform and got out of the bus at Planjo's house. There were policemen and soldiers there. At Planjo's house, the witness saw there were already male prisoners there from Svrake and Semizovac, about 113. The next day, the prison commander, whose name was Vlaco, ordered them all outside and asked who wanted to work. No one volunteered, so Vlaco himself picked out people. After that, when the prisoners were picked for work, squads were made up by lining the prisoners in front of the building and counting out the first 40 or 50 or 60 people. The witness names some people in uniform who came from the front lines to take detainees. Some were violent with the prisoners and beat the witness. The same person who took them up gave the detainees orders at the lines. They were told to do things like dig and cover trenches and communication trenches and dugouts, carry ammunition, cut wood, and carry the bodies of killed Serb forces from the battlefield. The witness was first used as a human shield on September 19 or 20, 1992. He learned from another prisoner who had also been a human shield the previous day with the witness's nephew -- that his nephew had been killed on the front line. The witness asked Vlaco whether there was a way to bring his nephew down from the battlefield, and that morning, Vlaco selected the witness to go to Zuc to look for him. There were about 40 detainees who went to work that day. The witness never got to pick up his nephew's body. One Dragan Damjanovic beat the witness and another man as they were forced to carry the body of someone else who had been killed down from the battlefield. Later, a team of soldiers arrived and the witness was taken with three other men. There were three soldiers behind him, two shooting over his shoulders while one pointed a gun barrel at his back. The same thing happened the next day. About ten days later, he was used again as a human shield. The witness was used as a human shield again at the beginning of October and once at the end of October. At the beginning of October, one Spiric Nebojsa, who was Vlaco's deputy, was one of the soldiers going behind him. The fifth time the witness was used as a human shield, they went to Ravne and there each prisoner had to carry a sack of sand behind him with a Serb soldier going a short distance behind. The soldier would order the prisoner to throw down the sack and the soldier would lie behind it and fire from there while the prisoner had to run back and get ammunition. The sixth time he was used as a human shield was at a location in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the direction of Golo Brdo. The line commander, one Zeljko Trifkovic, told the witnesses that special forces from Vogosca, Ilijas and Ilidza were all there. When the witness and other selected with him arrived, they were ordered to sing Serb songs. The witness was beaten by a member of the Serb police from Ilidza. Later the witness and one other prisoner were taken by special forces from Ilidza along a trail towards Golo Brdo. The witness was told to walk with the other prisoner, following in his footsteps to make sure there were no mines. His job was to watch for Bosnian military forces and warn the Serbs. The unit commander told the witness that if the Bosnian army fired first, the Serbs would kill them. On 8 February 1993, the witness and 35 others were taken to Kula. At Kula, the witness learned prisoners were there from Doboj, Manjaca and Grapska. One day the witness was coming from back from work at the line and told to collect two bodies lying on the side of the road. He knew both, recognising one as Zahid Barucija. Two days they were told to dig out Barucija and that his body would be exchanged. While he was being use as a human shield, the witness recalls that sometimes the Bosnian side would fire on them as they advanced. On the first occasion he was used as a shield, the witness saw the bodies of two men he recognised, also people killed by shrapnel while they were digging trenches. That concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make two observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are ready with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. The first observation is that the correction from the 8th to the 9th of February, having been made by the witness a few minutes ago in the statement, ought correspondingly to be made in the 89(F) summary. I don't think there will be any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see from your nodding, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, second?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not the biggest point in the case, Your Honour. The second observation is this: That the version of the 89(F) summary that was being read out by Ms. Edgerton is not the same as the version which I have in front of me. It's slightly fuller. I don't make any particular complaint. It's just that it's different, a question implicit in that, Your Honour, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, would the Prosecution take care in the future that the summary read out is the same as the one presented to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I certainly would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for the positive response on those points, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I've got one question for you in relation to this summary. I'm not quite sure that the transcript is correct, but right in the beginning, you said, according to the transcript, the night of the 28th of May, 1992, Gornja Bioca came under infantry fire. Yes, so I take it in the summary, the previous infantry fire, the shooting from infantry weapons is not to be considered as really infantry fire -- yes, I now I better understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's also my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make one other observation which I hope will be helpful. That was, and I make absolutely no complaint at all about this, rather the contrary, that's a slightly fuller 89(F) summary than we often have. That's a bit fuller than I had in front of me, of course. But it's -- but I don't complain about that at all. In fact, the Defence's position would be that it's helpful on the whole if the summary is as full as possible. It does lead to this, though: That so far that that's already been read out and the witness has already, in his evidence so far, confirmed these statements, we would be very supportive on the Defence side of avoidance of going over any of that ground again, as much as possible. This is not a witness -- there are witnesses in the other category. This is a witness, Your Honour, where the Defence is particularly insistent that these points are brought out orally in evidence. As long as they are clearly there on the record, we are not encouraging drawing out or going over this ground again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although, of course, reading the summary doesn't bring the summary into evidence because it's the statement that is in evidence, and the reading out of the 89(F) summary is mainly for the purpose of informing the public of what is tendered into evidence and what will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that isn't, clearly, entirely, correct. With respect, we agree with that. But we are in this position: That when the 89(F) summary is read before the witness gives his evidence, it becomes a little bit artificial when the witness has confirmed the statement. The 89(F) summary in detail is then based on that statement. If the witness then is -- if anybody seriously supposes that the witness is going to give evidence which radically departs from what we've heard now, well, frankly, that's a very unsatisfactory situation because that leaves a new 89(F) summary at the end to tell the public actually what he's said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that everyone is happy with how it went until now, so let's proceed, and we take proper notice of your observations, Mr. Stewart. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin with the clarifying questions from Mr. Selimovic, I just want to direct Your Honours, if I can, to Exhibit 527, because this witness's testimony relates to Ilijas municipality, and I believe in Exhibit 527, at page 29, you have a map of Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We even brought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour, has been looking at and marked a copy of a further map which is effectively a blow-up of a topographical map that covers the bottom -- can I say the south-eastern part of Ilijas municipality, as depicted on page 29, and, to a limited extent, the northern parts of Novi Grad municipality, as depicted on page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P557.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Selimovic, in the first paragraphs of your statements to the ICTY and your own authorities, you describe the village you came from, Gornja Bioca, and in your ICTY statement, you say your village was mixed but with a distinct Muslim and Serb part. Could you just tell the Court what were relations like between the Muslims and Serbs in your village in the years before the war?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I believe that the relations were good, because we went along well, we went to school together, went to play football together, went out dancing together. And I don't know how all these events came about in our village because I believe we ought to have protected each other rather than kill and slaughter each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what -- can you recall a time at which tensions between these two ethnic groups began to increase, a month, a year?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did things start to change?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Before the war, a month before the outbreak of the war when the barricades had already been set up. One of them was under the -- under a fly-over there and another one was under the bridge at Bioca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I just direct to the map of Ilijas and Vogosca areas that you have on the machine beside you, marked in blue. Did you make those markings yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you identified your village, Gornja Bioca, at number 1?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the location you marked at number two?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: The village of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the distance between your two villages?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Two and a half to three kilometres. There's a hill called Krstac between the two villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Donja Bioca, marked as number 3 on that map, a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: It's a Serb village. There were only two or three cottages that were owned by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, leaving the map for a moment, I want to ask some more questions about the statements you gave, some clarifying questions. On paragraph 5 of your statement to the Tribunal, you said that barricades appeared on the road from your village to Ilijas in March 1992. Were those the barricades you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that those people who manned the barricades wore a camouflage uniform. Do you recall what colour the uniform was?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Green, yellow and black. They also wore drab-olive uniforms. I saw Simo Crnogorac wearing one such uniform, a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "neighbour of yours", could you tell me where Simo Crnogorac came from?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Donja Bioca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- is he a Muslim or a Serb? Is that a Muslim or a Serb name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his occupation before the war, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: He worked at the ironworks. He was a plain worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on in your ICTY statement, in paragraph 6, you said that during the month or so, you stood guard around your village, you heard some big guns shooting from the direction of Paljevo. Is Paljevo the location you've indicated as number 7 on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Paljevo is not a village, it's a hill where, during World War II, in 1941 or 1942, there were some insurgents there. There is a plateau there that has quite a propensity for artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that the location you marked as number 7 on the map beside you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Paljevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, or could you see where the fire was directed to, in what direction the big guns were shooting at?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: There was shooting in the direction of Soko Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 8 of your statement to the ICTY, and throughout your statement, you use the word Chetniks. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber who you mean when you use that word?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: This term refers to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in both your 1993 statements and your statement to the ICTY, you speak of the killing of your brother, and in your earlier statement, you indicated your sister-in-law identified Srpko Pustivuk as the person responsible. Now, did you know this man, Pustivuk, before the war?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He grew up together with us. We played football together, and when we were going to different villages to play football matches, he'd join us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of job he worked at before the war?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: He completed his schooling and then started working as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Well, we know because we used to see him wearing a police uniform. He went with me to Ilijas on several occasions when I was on my way to work, and I would stop by at my workplace producing prefabricated houses, and he would go on in the direction of the municipality and then followed his work schedule. I don't know whether he worked in Sarajevo or in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Selimovic, after you were detained at the school in Bioca, did you then see Pustivuk, or did you not see him?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes. Once he came to the school, spent some five minutes there and went away. We never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I believe he was wearing a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 11 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about your capture and you say you were surrounded by people in camouflage uniforms and told you would have to go to the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to see any of the people who surrounded you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: No. We were unable to recognise them because they were some 300 or 400 metres away from us, outside a forest there in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who told you, then, that you would have to go to the school?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Refik Sehic and Zahid Sehic came and they told us we were to go to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are two Muslims who came; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, but they were taken prisoners the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that same paragraph, you say you recognised a man by the name of Cedo. Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, Cedo Pustivuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he any relation, to your knowledge, to Srpko Pustivuk?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Srpko is a relative of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 12 of your statement to the Tribunal, you say that there were about 60 of you on your arrival at the primary school in Bioca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know most of those people by face or by name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, they were all relatives of mine, friends, neighbours, from Bioca. There was only one person from Crnotina, Huso Abdziaglic [phoen]; his nickname was Dzenadil [phoen], I believe, and the other was his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know the ethnicity of those people that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: You mean those that were detained? They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you under guard when you were at the primary school? Were there guards there?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, of course there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of those guards by face or by name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Not some of them. I knew all of them because they were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- did you know them, then, to be Serb or Muslim or something else?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Serbs. What else would they be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 of your ICTY statement, you talk about the men who transferred you to Podlugovi. Where did they come from, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I didn't know the people. I know that they wore camouflage uniforms and had socks on their heads. They had slits for the eyes and then some of them also had one for the mouth; others didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Podlugovi, when you got there, you found a large number of people already there divided among three rooms. Did you know most of those people by face or by name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I only knew Zlatko Bece, and one other person from Ljesevo, Husein, but I don't know his last name. We became acquainted later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic background of these people that you became acquainted with?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: There were Muslims, one or two Croats. I only knew Zlatko Bece, who died, who was brought over from the railway station where they had thrown a smoke grenade at them. And Sehic Menso was also brought over with Zlatko who died that very night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to turn to the map beside you, is Podlugovi the location you've marked as number 4 on the map?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded when you were at Podlugovi?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I didn't know these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from the way they spoke, for example, whether or not they were of Serb background?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you determine that?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: We found this out from Slavko, and we knew. Who else could it have been but Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 of your statement from 1993, you say, "They took away Mensur Sehic," who you've already mentioned, "and Hamdija Drmic, and Drmic was never seen again." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: He was taken by Mladjo Maksimovic, also known as Nikola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Maksimovic a Muslim or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he was taken away by Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw who?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I saw Nikola and Hamdija as they went into the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your statement, you refer to the man by the name of Vasilja Stolica. Is he a Muslim or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, I worked at the company producing prefabricated houses, and he worked in the heater room that was part of the company that I worked for, Kotlana [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on in time to August of 1992 in paragraph 20 of your statement to the ICTY, and paragraph 23 of your earlier statement, you talk about a man who introduced himself as the Minister of Justice. Had you ever seen him before he came to Podlugovi?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again after that?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, once. This was at Svrake, at the building there, where he came and asked us how we were, how we were doing, and that was the last time we saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed that second time?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: He was bearing clothes that were blue in colour, a light blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How had you heard, because you talk about it in those same paragraphs, that Svrake and Semizovac had been occupied?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: We heard shooting and shelling over there, and then we heard it on the radio, that it had fallen and that the Serbian forces had taken over Semizovac and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the map that's beside you that you've marked, did you indicate Semizovac at point number 5 and Svrake at point number 6?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, next I'd just like to talk to you about your arrival at Planjo's house, and the paragraph is paragraph number 22 in your statement to the Tribunal, and I'd like to show you a photograph, it's previously Prosecution Exhibit 379. Now, you've got the images in front of you, Mr. Selimovic, on the computer screen and beside you. Now, looking at that photo, which bears the number 03616938 in the top right-hand corner, can you tell me whether you recognise the building?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was in there. Of course I recognise it. We were in this building in the cellar downstairs, and some of the inmates were in this building on the ground floor. And the room was divided in two by a table, so in one part of the room, we would sleep and in the other part of the room, we would be served food. Upstairs, on the first floor, there were women and children. There was music there and probably the guards were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that this was the next detention facility you were taken to after you left the facility in Podlugovi?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you read numbers, you better do it slowly otherwise they appear wrong on the screen. There's no risk here because it's Exhibit 379, but an eight-digit number suddenly becomes a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nine-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 4 between the 3 and the 8 should not be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, does this location depicted on this photograph have a name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: It was called Planina's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it look like -- in this photograph, does it look to you like it did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't recall seeing these windows on the roof up there because we were never allowed to really take a good look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned just now, and also mentioned in paragraph 23 of your ICTY statement, that there were women and children in the building. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: They would come to have dinner or lunch. When we were there, they would also come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of those women or children?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I knew only one woman, Ferida Terzic, who brought us food. She didn't bring food to us, she brought food to Ferid, and he shared his with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she one of the women that you were speaking up who were in the upstairs of the building in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other women in this upstairs of Planjo's house that you knew?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: There were women. There was a Serbian woman who married a Muslim man. She had a young son. She was with them as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 23 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about the male prisoners from Semizovac and Vogosca who you found at Planjo's house.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were at Planjo's house for some time. Did you become acquainted with a number of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes. Zajid Barucija, Esad Mracevic [phoen], Hido Ahmed and some others whose names I can't remember. There was man called Halilovic, but I am not sure. There were some people from the village above Semizovac, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of these detainees to be Serb?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: When we were supposed to be transferred to Kula, a month before that, Boro Margetic was brought there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, to your knowledge, there was one Serb at Planjo's house?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the ethnic background of the rest of the detainees there?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: They were Muslims. There were also Croats there. There was one Croat with us, Zvonko Puharic was his name, and he was also taken away. I don't know whether he was taken to Kula together with us or later, but as soon as he was brought in, he was put in a car and then I saw him again in Kula. His name was Zvonko Puharic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Selimovic, you were guarded while you were at Planjo's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the entrance here under the terrace. This is where a guard was standing and this is where we entered, and there was one guard below by the gate. That's where we would go to descend into the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your guards, did you know them to be Muslims or Serbs or something else?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: They were Serbs. What else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I know because one was called Ljubisa. Now, I don't know his last name. Another one was called Delipara. The third one was Vlado Mrzlic. This guy Delipara, this was his last name; I don't know his first name. There was Momir Damjanovic, who was also a Serb. And for the others, I can't remember their names. I didn't know their names to start with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct if I tell you that I understand you're saying you knew they were Serbs because you got to know them by name?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were the guards at Planjo's house in uniform?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did you see them in?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour of camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Green, yellow and black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at one document, Mr. Selimovic, bearing the ERN number 0297-7353 -- 0297-7353, dated 30 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you're ready, if we could have the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Prosecution Exhibit P558.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, I'd like you to direct your attention to the last paragraph of that document and the name list. Do you see the name of Bego Selimovic on that document?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any comment about this document and why your name is on it?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose that they were drawing up lists as we were taken to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask you another way. Do you recognise the other names that appear on this document with yours?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I do. They were with me in the prison, all of them, and we were taken to work together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And are these Muslim names that appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not able to see an English copy of the document so I'm a bit paralysed.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, this document lists you and seven other people as being taken to work as Zuc on the 30th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to work, but I can't remember the date. It was a horrible time. I can't remember every detail. But we were taken to work every day; sometimes to Zuc, sometimes to Ravne or to Rajlovac. Wherever we were taken, we had to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this document could reflect the time that you were taken for work from the detention facility; is that what I'm understanding from you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've named some locations where you were taken to work at. Could you describe the type of work you had to do.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: We had to dig trenches, we had to do the filling, we covered trenches, we had to pull out the fallen Serbian soldiers. When they needed people for human shields, they would use us. And then when we returned, oftentimes we would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, at paragraph 26 of your ICTY statement, you name some people who you say took you from the detention facility up to the lines. The first name you give is a man called Milosevic. Could you tell us who Milosevic was?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I don't know who he was. He was a soldier. He would come and take 20, 30, 40 or 50 men and took them to work. He would take them to work and bring them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dusan Arnaut, who was he?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I believe that he was a soldier, just like the previous one, Milosevic. He also came to take workers. He would take us to work and he would bring us back. In the meantime, he would guard us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Damjanovic?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Damjanovic, wherever we were taken, he would follow and he would beat us. He would beat whoever he saw. If he didn't see us, he wouldn't beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the previous two names as you've identified as soldiers. Was Damjanovic also a soldier, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: He was a soldier, but I don't know what role he played. Sometimes he arrived in a camouflage uniform and other times in a black uniform. He had a long beard, long hair. Sometimes he wore a black hat with a cockade, and sometimes he also carried a flag with the inscription Chetniks on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it, or could I ask you, these three men who you've just spoken about, were they Serbs or Muslims or something else?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about the first time you were used as a human shield on Zuc hill. Is Zuc the -- if you could have another look at the map that was beside you on the machine, can you see, although it's been chopped off a little bit in the reproduction, can you see the location you marked as number 8, which was the first time you were used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Here, on Zuc? From Zuc towards Orlic or towards Kmetisce [phoen], there is a playground there and some oak trees, and this is where I was used as a human shield for the first time. That time, there was no shooting. So on the following day, I was also used as a human shield, and a further 50 metres was taken towards Kmetisce on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on further in your statement to the Tribunal, at paragraph 34, you talk about the occasion when you were used as a human shield at the end of October, and you say, at that time, two Serb soldiers were going behind you. One was Spiric Nebojsa, and you say that he was Vlaco's deputy, Vlaco being the man you identified earlier in your statement as the commander of Planjo's house. How did you learn that Spiric was Vlaco's deputy?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: On several occasions, he told us that. He said that if Vlaco wasn't there, that he was our commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, before we get any problem, you say in reproducing number 8 it disappears from the map, but you tendered a copy where number 8 does not appear either. So perhaps for the record, I think there is a problem in tendering a reproduction, but then to clarify the issue, we find on the bottom right-hand side, almost south from where it reads Vogosca, the city we see at the very edge of the reproduced map, the word Zuc, and that's where the 8 was marked, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. Just your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour, because I think we are nearing the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, yes, because if you say you could finish in a couple of minutes, then we'll continue; otherwise, it would be the time for a break. But if you say it's a matter of not more than five to seven minutes, then with the assistance of the interpreters and the technicians, we could continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now Mr. Selimovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it won't be any more than five or seven minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in paragraph 37 of your statement to the Tribunal, you talk about being asked to bury Zahid Barucija. Do you have any idea of the month in which you were asked to do this?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I remember, it was in January 1993, between the 22nd and the 25th of January. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who he was beforehand?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Zahid Barucija?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Planjo's house. He was brought in as a worker. He was brought in to lay some logs, together with Dragan Damjanovic and Borisa. These two brought him, and they did not -- we didn't see him alive again. On the following day, as we were working, we were told that Barucija started running and that he stepped on a landmine and that he got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further question for you now, Mr. Selimovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, we will first have a break, and after the break - I take it that, Mr. Stewart, you will cross-examine the witness - so after the break, questions will be put to you by Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. We will adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, in paragraph 6 of the statement that you gave to this Tribunal, you refer to keeping guard and you're organising yourselves. You said there were eight guard posts, two men on each post, and you said that your weapons were your own hunting rifles. Did you own a hunting rifle before you started to keep guard?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you one of the men who bought a weapon subsequently?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you buy?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: An M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in your statement, later you had some weapons that you bought. First of all, when did you -- do you remember exactly when you started to keep guard, you personally?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 3rd or on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you bought that M-48 before or after you started to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: We were standing guard even before we had rifles. We had only one hunting rifle. And later on, Smajo Durmic sold me a rifle. He asked me to pay him 300 German marks. I don't know who he himself had gotten this rifle from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you started, as you say, to keep guard yourself on the 3rd or the 4th of May, how long after that did you buy that rifle?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 2nd of May or maybe on the 3rd of May. But even before that, for two or three nights before that, we were standing guard with one hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer in your statement to you, and that's you and somebody else, because you talk about "we had some weapons that we bought, as well, two automatic rifles and two or three M-48 military rifles." Those weapons, those were for the group that was on your particular guard post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: No. I was standing guard with my own rifle, and there was also a hunting rifle owned by Taib Dzogo. We took turns but we used the same weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had two automatic rifles and two or three M-48 military rifles?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Hamdija Durmic had an M-48, Mustafa Hadzic had an automatic rifle that he had bought, and I don't know who had the other automatic rifle. I know that there were some hunting rifles on top of these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You keep talking about the hunting rifles, but, Mr. Selimovic, I'm asking you because it is your statement that says, "We bought two automatic rifles and two or three M-48 military rifles." So far, you have told the Trial Chamber that Mustafa Hadzic had an automatic rifle, you don't know who had the other automatic rifle, and you had, you've told the Trial Chamber, an M-48. So somebody else as well had an M-48, did they?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Hamdija Durmic had an M-48; I've said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite right. The transcript got a bit blurred there. Those men, were they together with you on your guard post?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Not all of us. There were two men at one guard post, two other men were at another guard post, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was on your guard post with you?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: There was myself, my cousin, Mirsad Selimovic, Ramiz Hamzic, who replaced us, and Ferid Hamzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's none of the men that you mentioned a minute ago as the owners of this other M-48 and the two automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: That's correct. Dzogo Taib had a hunting rifle. He was an elderly man. He couldn't stand guard himself. That's why he gave his rifle to somebody else. And there was also my rifle, the one that I had bought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was your rifle the one that -- yes, your rifle, was that the only rifle available on your particular guard post?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: Yes, my rifle and the hunting rifle that belonged to Taib Dzogo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your statement when you talk about "we had some weapons that we bought," what group is it that you're referring to there as "we"?

utterances.speaker: Bego Selimovic
utterances.text: I was referring to myself and to Hamdija Durmic, because Smajo Durmic brought these two rifles and sold them to the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does any question arise from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions for you either, Mr. Selimovic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. Of course the Court has read your statements as well, so the information you have provided is not only the answers to the questions put to you today but the statements will be available for the Court as well, which, of course, give us more information than you've just told us today. Mr. Selimovic, I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and to answer the questions of the parties, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just take a sip of water, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one residual matter, then, that arises in relation to this witness's evidence which didn't require him to remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then hear that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it relates to the point that Your Honours raised immediately before the evidence began, at the tail end of the statements relating to events outside the indictment period. Your Honour mentioned the limits of a criminal case. There is, of course, also the limits of how far a witness has a say over what evidence gets admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. We're at one on that, with respect, Your Honour. In our submission, Your Honours, having explored it with Ms. Edgerton, it's quite clear that this is -- this piece of the evidence is not linked to evidence within the indictment period sufficiently closely for it to be properly admitted, and that, therefore, should be excluded, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to take a strong position in this regard. I also advised the Court that I didn't make any redactions at the specific wish of Mr. Selimovic, whose confidence in and understanding of the 89(F) proceedings was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is expected to take out, since the Chamber will not admit it, take out any specific events in January and February 1993, Ms. Edgerton. The practical way is how they are going to do that because to produce even more paper might be not a good thing to do. What we'll do is, the Chamber will instruct the Registry to strike out those parts of the statement we have in mind, and then the parties will get a copy of that specific page where we find any errors. If there would then be any further problem, we will hear from the parties. The Chamber, at the same time, appreciated to receive P558, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. double-side copied, because the waste of paper is not to be ignored in this Tribunal, and especially these one-page documents could be printed out in B/C/S on one side. The only problem for Madam Registrar is that one side of the page would then have P558 and the other side of the page would then be P558.1, but I think we would overcome this problem. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like say, Your Honour, I can take absolutely no credit in that regard, and pass it all on to Ms. Javier beside me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it the one who took the initiative will take the credit for it as well. Is there any other issue at this moment? Because otherwise I would like to, first of all, go through the exhibits in relation to this witness, and then to the extent the parties are prepared, also to pay attention to the Djokanovic document -- exhibits which have been prepared, more or less. I saw that there was at least a list of documents produced so that we can go through that as well. First of all, the exhibits in relation to this witness. Madam Registrar, could you perhaps briefly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar justly wanted me to make the redaction first before the documents are admitted into evidence. I'm just seeking the assistance of the parties. It is the 1990 -- no, I think it's the ICTY statement ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it perhaps logically starts with the other one because it has the specific dates, and then I believe it's very clear in the other statement which events follow on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I would like -- since I now see the originals, Ms. Edgerton, what you tendered as P556, there is still, if I may say so, the old version of the 1993 statement attached to it. Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we're not relying on the old version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless, as you presented it, it's now part of P556 so what we would like to have to be P556 is just the statement without anything attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that starts with last three digits 973 and goes on until 980 in the English translation, and it would be 915, last three digits, up to 922 in the B/C/S original, or we never know what the original is but at least the -- yes. Madam Registrar, if you would. Yes, so we take the 1993 statement ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We think it's paragraph 32 onwards is the earlier statement and 39 onwards in the other statement. I don't know if that's the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not our problem. We would like to have a clean copy tendered of the ICTY statement without the attachment and also a clean copy of the better, legible version, and I think that's P555, but to have a clean copy separated from anything else. Could you provide that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, I hadn't realised what the particular hold-up was, I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next step would be to take out, I think, 31 and 32, as you suggested. Since the 1993 statement was P555, if I do not -- if I'm not mistaken, yes, we'll take it out from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't pressing for 31 because I think 31 does, in fact, strictly speaking, relate back to 1992. If not, the -- the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not very clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I really don't mind either way, Your Honour, on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take out the last line -- no, let's take out 32. I think that's a more proper way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 32 onwards, Your Honour, as we would understand it. I think Ms. Edgerton is nodding in apparent agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's unclear a bit. Ms. Edgerton, do you have any -- for example, 34 is about the detention in Svrake, which might well be within the time limits. The next one, however, 35, would be in the Kula camp which would be on from the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, it isn't quite that simple anyway. The sentence, "During my detention in Svrake, I was beaten up by a Chetnik," and so on, that may very well stay in, but the rest of it then relates again to Kula as to what did and didn't happen in Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take out paragraph 32, Ms. Edgerton, if you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 32 is taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 33 can also be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 33 is taken out, then, as well. I thank you. Then 34, first line -- the first sentence could remain and the rest to be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 35 can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 35 to be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the last paragraph, anyhow. Madam Registrar, this is then P555, and P556 would then be the ICTY statement without any attachment but with translation. Yes, so redactions, do the parties still need a copy of the pages, or is that clear enough, what I removed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's clear enough, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That saves another two sheets of paper. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P555 is the witness statement to Republic of BiH, Ilijas municipality commission for crime investigation, dated 5 April 1993, a point 1 is the English translation. P556 is the ICTY witness statement, dated June 21, 1997, and point 1 is the B/C/S translation. P557 is the map of Ilijas and Vogosca and surrounding area that was pre-marked by the witness. And P558, daily bulletin for August 29, 1992, Serbian Republic of BiH, Serbian municipality of Vogosca branch prison, and point 1 is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, objections, Your Honour. Perhaps I lost track of it Your Honour, but I'm not sure that we dealt with the equivalent removal of paragraphs from the ICTY -- from the ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any -- I'm not quite sure whether there are any equivalent --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was 39 onwards, Your Honour. It wasn't too long after that that we were taken to Kula. Those are the exactly equivalent events, and the Defence proposal is that then there's no -- there's nothing interspersed there. The whole of the rest of that statement comes out as all relating to Kula and subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45 are to be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can we take out number 36? Because the corresponding paragraph has been removed from the 1993 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We certainly don't oppose that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then 36 is taken out, and it's clearly in the record that these documents that had not yet been filed, although were admitted, the parts just mentioned are now taken out and are no longer in evidence anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And no doubt the public will appreciate when they peruse the transcript and look at the 89(F) statement, they will realise that the tail end of the 89(F) statement relates to evidence which has been taken out of the case, so they will put it out of their minds as they avidly read that bit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if they follow all of the transcript, they have not only heard the resume but also the remarks just made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just to raise something, in complete fairness, that we may have overlooked. There is one episode in which the witness was a human shield that looks like it's occurred in January of 1993, and in all fairness, I thought I better raise it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's paragraph 38 of his ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please. I raise this, Your Honour, because he testified, and from the totality of his statements, it's quite clear that he was a human shield on the sixth occasion, found the body of Barucija immediately after that, and within four days, two days - he's changed his story a couple of times - but in any case, a very short while, was transferred to Kula. So it seems to me we're talking about a time in January 1993. And I apologise for not raising it earlier. I certainly had not appreciated it until ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear. If we have got five occasions, could we consider that this was not the end of it? I mean, it doesn't add that much, it doesn't -- Mr. Stewart, do you insist on this precision?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are two points, Your Honour.
